groups.text: A class file is a byte array with a fixed layout.
The first four bytes are always CAFEBABE.
Then the minor and major version: zeroxforty-one is sixty-five, which means Java twenty-one.
Then the size of the constant pool.
In the pool, each entry starts with a tag, and the tag decides how many bytes follow.
So to find anything after the pool, you walk every entry.
And every J D K adds a major version.
Frameworks shipped their own ASM, and a release for each one.
Since J D K twenty-four, the J D K has its own library for it: the ClassFile A P I.
Its parse method turns the bytes into a ClassModel: an immutable description of the class.
A model is a sequence of elements: methods, fields and attributes.
Open a method's code, and you get more elements: one typed object per instruction.
And it's lazy.
A part is parsed only when you open it.
Building runs the other way.
You pass lambdas, and each one gets a builder.
The CodeBuilder has one method per instruction.
Each call emits one element, and build turns them into bytes.
To change a class, a transform hands each element of the old class to the new class's builder.
Pass it through with builder.with, and it comes out unchanged.
Call nothing, and it's dropped.
A code transform does the same with instructions.
Call other builder methods, and you replace it: ldc two hundred ninety becomes ldc three hundred ten.
It's a flatMap: each element in, zero, one or more out.
FeeRuleVtwo's fee now returns three thousand eight hundred seventy-five instead of three thousand six hundred twenty-five.
In code, it's a lambda that gets the builder and one element.
Kotlin calls the same Java A P I.
The rule. A class is a sequence of elements.
Parse reads them, build writes them, and a transform maps each one to zero or more.
Quick check. For ldc two hundred ninety, a code transform calls with on the element, then ldc three hundred ten.
What does the new code hold?
Both. ldc two hundred ninety, then ldc three hundred ten.
One element in, two out.
